editorial.headline: Legal Consulting: Nationally Open, but Off-Limits to Foreign Nationals in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans company-formation documents and legal instruments, yet Bali’s professional rule closes the registration path to foreign nationals.
editorial.body:
Legal consulting under this activity is document-centred work with real consequences for how organisations are formed and governed. Its scope includes preparing legal documents, documents for legal entities, cooperation agreements and similar instruments connected with company formation. It also reaches the preparation of notarial deeds, wills, trusts and related materials, alongside other legal-document work. The record further identifies the activity with a law office: this is a professional legal-services setting, not merely administrative support around paperwork.

The activity is open nationally across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. At the national level it is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In practical terms, the national investment classification does not impose a foreign-share cap below full ownership for this activity. That national position is important, but it is not the whole answer for a founder choosing Bali as the place of registration.

In Bali, the answer is direct: a foreign national cannot register this activity for PMA today. The Bali status is TERTUTUP because legal services are reserved for advocates licensed in Indonesia. Although the national KBLI catalogue records the code as open, the profession itself is off-limits to foreign nationals under the rule cited in the record. This is not a minor local qualification on an otherwise usable foreign-investment route; it determines whether the activity can be registered by a foreigner in Bali.

Bali also maintains a permanent, island-wide block on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, as set out in the Governor’s letter cited in the record. That province-wide rule forms part of the wider Bali setting, while this activity’s stated closure rests specifically on the Indonesian-licensed-advocate requirement. Founders should therefore read the national 100% ceiling accurately: it describes the national classification, not a permission to bypass the professional restriction that closes this activity to foreign nationals in Bali.
editorial.pullQuote: A national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling does not override Bali’s closure of legal services to foreign nationals.
